title: Collagen for Lifters: What the Evidence Supports and What It Does Not
titleDe: Kollagen für Kraftsportler: Was die Evidenz stützt und was nicht
idCoverage: 15 of 16 sources with PMID (the 16th is the ClinicalTrials.gov registry search)
warnings: Tendon section graded weak and conflicting: two positive 5 g/day trials (Jerger 2022, 2023) vs. one null 15 g/day trial (Balshaw 2023); the meta-analysis rates tendon evidence 'very low' certainty.
Most tendon and joint trials are small and several tested branded 'specific collagen peptide' products (Praet 2019 names TENDOFORTE); I did not verify funding or industry ties study by study.
Vitamin C timing evidence is a blood marker only (Shaw 2017, n=8; Lee 2024, n=10) and the two disagree on whether 15 g is enough; no graded trial measured injury rates.
Zdzieblik 2015 (sarcopenic men) used a silica placebo with no protein, so the article frames it as 'some protein beats none', not a win for collagen.
The trial count (9) comes from a broad ClinicalTrials.gov search and includes one observational study and one undenatured type II collagen (NT-II) trial; worth a glance.

DE compliance: the EU has no authorised health claim for collagen itself (only vitamin C 'contributes to normal collagen formation'); the article makes no product claims, but keep this in mind for any linked deals copy.
